prompt:
# Write one behaviour-tree node that ADJUSTS an existing navigator

You are writing a single node for the behaviour tree of a Unitree Go2 quadruped
navigating an indoor space it has no map of.

Below the node is an inherited, pretrained, **frozen** locomotion policy. The
only thing anything ever sends the robot is a Twist — `(vx, vy, wz)`. You never
touch the policy, the gait, or the joints.

**You are not writing the navigator.** A navigator already exists, it already
drives, and it will keep driving whether or not your node does anything. Your
node sits above it and revises what it asked for.

Return **one Python module**, in one fenced ```python block, and nothing else
that looks like code. Everything you want to say in prose, say outside the
fence. What the module must contain is set out in "What to return" at the end.

## How the tree runs: a layered command pipeline

Every node in the tree ticks, **every step, in order**. Nothing short-circuits
anything.

    Layer[ ports, BASE, node_1, node_2, ... ]
             ^      ^      ^
             |      |      `- each may revise the fields it declared
             |      `-------- proposes a whole command, every tick
             `--------------- publishes a few facts from the sensors

The **base** is a general indoor navigator. It gets the robot most of the way
most of the time, it handles the awkward cases, and it never declines to act.
Each later node may then adjust individual fields of what the base proposed.

This is subsumption: a competent low layer, refined by narrow higher ones. Your
node is one of the higher ones.

**So the thing you are writing is small.** It does one thing to one part of the
command, under one condition, and the rest of the time it stays out of the way.

## The one hard rule: you declare which fields you may write

Your class declares `WRITES` — the Twist fields it is allowed to touch:

```python
WRITES = ("vx",)            # may bound or set forward speed, nothing else
WRITES = ("wz",)            # may steer, but may not change speed
WRITES = ("vx", "wz")       # both. Only if the mechanism genuinely needs both.
```

This is **enforced, not advisory.** Writing a field you did not declare raises
immediately and the node is rejected. Declare the smallest set your mechanism
actually needs — a node that declares all three is claiming to be a navigator,
and it will be judged as one.

Two ways to write, and they are the only two:

```python
ports.cap(vx=0.35)       # min(|pending|, 0.35), sign kept. Never speeds up.
ports.adjust(wz=0.8)     # replaces the field outright. Last writer wins.
```

Prefer `cap` whenever the mechanism is a limit, a bound, or a "no faster than"
— it composes with other caps in any order, which `adjust` does not.

And you can see what the base asked for:

```python
pending = ports.command          # a Command(vx, vy, wz). Never None when you
                                 # tick, because the base ticks before you.
if pending.vx > my_limit:
    ports.cap(vx=my_limit)
```

**Do not call `ports.drive(...)`.** That writes the whole command and is the
base's job; it raises for a node that narrowed `WRITES`.

## Declining is a first-class outcome, and it is free

Return `Status.FAILURE` from `precondition`, or simply write nothing in `tick`,
and the base's command passes through **byte-identical**. The robot behaves
exactly as if your node were not in the tree.

That matters more than it sounds. Your node's contribution is measured by adding
it to the tree and re-running the same worlds: it can only be credited for the
episodes it changes, and it is blamed for every episode it breaks. A node that
acts only when its trigger genuinely holds is a good node. A node that fires on
every tick has replaced the base rather than supported it, and it will be
measured as having done so.

## The node contract

A leaf is one of three kinds, and the kind is the class you subclass:

- **`Condition`** — answers one question about the world and publishes it as a
  port. Never touches the Twist.
- **`Action`** — the only kind that may touch the Twist. With a narrowed
  `WRITES` it is a *modifier*, which is what you are writing.
- **`Decorator`** — wraps exactly one child and governs whether the child runs.
  Never touches the Twist itself.

Your class declares, as class attributes:

| Attribute | What it is |
|---|---|
| `WRITES` | the Twist fields this node may write. See above. |
| `PORTS` | a tuple of `Port` — the typed interface between nodes. See below. |
| `PRECONDITION` | one sentence: when this node applies |
| `EFFECT` | one sentence: what this node changes |
| `TAGS` | a tuple of short strings, for retrieval |

and implements:

```python
def reset(self, scenario, rng):    # clear per-episode state. optional.
def precondition(self, obs, ports) -> bool:   # default: always True
def tick(self, obs, ports) -> Status:         # Status.SUCCESS / FAILURE / RUNNING
```

**One precondition and one effect.** A node that needs two of either is two
nodes. This is not a style rule: contribution is measured by adding one node at
a time, and a node with two effects is attributable to neither.

**No coupling to a specific scenario.** Your node will be run on procedurally
generated worlds you have never seen. It may not name a room, a coordinate, a
doorway or a map. Anything it knows about the world it learns through `obs` at
tick time.

### Ports

Ports are how nodes pass information to each other. They are **not** a
blackboard: at tick time you are handed a `PortView` restricted to exactly the
ports you declared, and touching anything else raises immediately.

```python
Port(name, PortType.X, Direction.IN)    # you read it:   value = ports["name"]
Port(name, PortType.X, Direction.OUT)   # you write it:  ports["name"] = value
```

The port vocabulary is **closed**. These seven types and no others:

| `PortType` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `POSE` | `(x, y, yaw)` — a belief about where the robot is, never ground truth |
| `BEARING` | radians, robot frame unless the port name says otherwise |
| `SPEED` | m/s, non-negative |
| `RANGES` | an array of beam returns, metres |
| `CONFIDENCE` | `[0, 1]` — how much to trust something |
| `FLAG` | a boolean fact about the episode |
| `REGION` | an area of the floor, `(x, y, radius)` |

Three ports are always published before your node ticks, so you may declare any
of them as inputs: `goal_known` (FLAG), `pose` (POSE), `ranges` (RANGES).
Anything else you declare as an input must be published by another node earlier
in the Layer, and if nothing does, the tree refuses to build.

Publish an OUT port when the quantity you computed is genuinely useful to
someone else — a limit, a bearing, a confidence. Do not publish your own
internal state.

### What to import

Exactly these, and nothing else.

```python
import math
import numpy as np

from core.observation import Command
from nodes.contract import (Action, Condition, Decorator, Direction, Port,
                            PortType, Status)
```

Import only what you use. You will usually not need `Command` at all: a modifier
revises fields, it does not construct commands.

### What your node can see

`tick` is handed an `Observation`, frozen, one per control step:

```python
obs.t                   # sim seconds since the episode started
obs.ranges              # np.ndarray, 181 beams, metres, inf where no return
obs.range_angles        # np.ndarray, beam bearings in the ROBOT frame, radians
obs.range_max           # 6.0 — what "as far as I can see" means
obs.pose_estimate       # (x, y, yaw) — the BELIEF about our pose, not the truth
obs.pose_error_estimate # scalar, metres — how wrong we think the belief is
obs.contact             # bool — are we touching something right now
obs.goal                # (x, y), or None meaning NOT DISCLOSED
```

Two of these are traps and both are deliberate:

- **`pose_estimate` is a belief.** On some scenarios a seeded random walk is
  added to it and it drifts away from the truth. Ground truth is never in
  `Observation`; the runner keeps it for scoring only.
- **`obs.goal` may be `None`**, meaning the goal exists and the episode is still
  scored against it, but this robot has not found it yet. It **latches**: once
  disclosed it stays disclosed. Your node runs on scenarios that withhold the
  goal and on scenarios that do not, so **handle `None` explicitly**. Do not
  assume a tuple.

The scan is 181 beams over a full circle, so `obs.ranges[0]` is not the front —
find the beam you want through `obs.range_angles`.

Speeds are saturated by the runner to `|vx|, |vy| <= 0.8 m/s` and
`|wz| <= 1.0 rad/s`. Asking for more is not an error; it is just clipped.

## The task family this node has to be useful for

Reach a goal whose position is known, in an indoor space with no map. Walls and furniture occlude; the route is not a straight line and the obstruction is often not visible until the robot is close to it.

## What to base the node on

A principle card has been written for this task. **Implement this principle and
nothing else.**

```yaml
id: gap_clipped_goal_bearing
node_name: SteerThroughWidestAdmissibleGap

mechanism: When the straight line to the goal is occluded, a purely goal-directed heading command drives the robot into the occluder and a purely repulsive one drives it away from the goal; both fail at the same places, namely openings (doorways, furniture gaps, corridor mouths) that are narrower than the obstacle beside them. The mechanism replaces the commanded heading with the *free-space-clipped* goal heading: from the current scan, extract the maximal contiguous angular intervals of beams that are free to at least the depth the robot needs to turn through them; discard those whose chord is narrower than the body plus a safety margin; and command the bearing inside the surviving interval that is angularly closest to the goal, held at least one body-clearance away from either edge of that interval. This helps for two reasons. First, it turns a local occlusion into an implicit subgoal — the opening — without any map, so the robot commits to a traversable aperture instead of grinding along the obstacle face. Second, because the aim bearing is pushed off the interval edges by the angle that a body-radius subtends at the aperture depth, the robot passes through the middle of an opening rather than clipping its jamb, which raises the closest approach distance in exactly the situations (narrow apertures) where it is smallest. The rule reads geometry only from the lidar, in the robot frame; the drifting pose estimate enters solely as a bearing preference.

trigger: Applies when (a) `goal` is not None, i.e. the goal position has been disclosed or latched, AND (b) the goal-bearing corridor is obstructed: the minimum finite range over beams within +/-0.43 rad of the goal bearing is below 1.2 m, AND (c) at least one admissible gap (defined in the derivation) exists in the forward half-plane. If (a) fails the node returns FAILURE without commanding (a goal-unknown explorer owns that case); if (b) fails the node returns FAILURE so that an unobstructed straight-line pursuit node keeps control; if (c) fails the node returns FAILURE so that a recovery/backtrack node takes over. The node never returns SUCCESS on its own — it returns RUNNING while it is steering, and the tree's goal-reached condition terminates it.

derivation: All numbers below are mine; none come from a source.
Frame and inputs. Wrap all bearings to (-pi, pi]. Sort beams by `range_angles`. Treat `inf` and any range > `range_max` as exactly range_max = 6.0 m for free-space tests and for width computation (an unreturned beam is free, not unknown, at this range). Beam spacing is 2*pi/181 = 0.0347 rad (~2.0 deg).
Goal bearing. theta_g = wrap(atan2(gy - y, gx - x) - yaw) using `pose_estimate` = (x, y, yaw). Only the bearing is consumed, never the range, and it is recomputed every step in the robot frame, so `pose_estimate` drift perturbs the *preference* by at most asin(min(1, pose_error_estimate / D)) radians at goal distance D and never corrupts the geometry: the gap edges, widths and clearances come from the scan alone. No pose history is integrated, so drift cannot accumulate inside this node.
Body scale. A Go2 standing is about 0.70 m long, 0.31 m wide. Circumscribed radius sqrt(0.35^2 + 0.155^2) = 0.38 m, rounded to r_body = 0.40 m. Safety margin 0.15 m gives r_clear = 0.55 m as the lateral half-width the robot wants around its commanded line.
Depth thresholds from the actuation limits given. The tightest arc the frozen policy can be asked for is v/w = 0.8 / 1.0 = 0.8 m radius. To swing the commanded heading off an obstacle that lies on the goal bearing, the robot therefore needs about 0.8 m of turning room plus its own 0.4 m radius: d_block = 1.2 m. That is the corridor-obstructed test in the trigger. Its angular half-width is atan(r_clear / d_block) = atan(0.55 / 1.2) = 0.43 rad (~25 deg). A beam counts as *free* for gap construction if its range is at least d_free = 1.5 m — d_block plus 0.3 m, so the robot does not commit to an aperture that closes at exactly the distance it needs to turn.
Gap construction. Restrict to the forward half-plane |phi| <= pi/2; gaps behind the robot would require reversing the direction of travel, which belongs to a backtracking node, not this one. Take maximal runs of consecutive free beams. For a run spanning [phi_lo, phi_hi] with angular extent dphi = phi_hi - phi_lo, let d_eval = min(range at phi_lo, range at phi_hi, 3.0) — the min makes the width estimate conservative, and the 3.0 m cap stops a distant run from being credited with a width the 2.0 deg beam spacing cannot resolve. Chord width w = 2 * d_eval * sin(dphi / 2).
Admissibility. Require w >= w_min = 0.60 m. Derivation: the robot needs its 0.31 m width plus roughly 0.145 m either side to pass an aperture head-on without the margin being smaller than a foot placement. 0.60 m is below the 0.76-0.90 m of ordinary interior doorways, so real openings survive the test, while slots narrower than the body (chair legs, table-to-wall slivers) are rejected. w_min < 2*r_clear = 1.10 m deliberately: r_clear is what the robot *wants*, w_min is what it can *fit through*, and refusing to fit through doorways would defeat the mechanism.
Selection and aim. Among admissible gaps choose the one minimising |wrap(phi_c - theta_g)| where phi_c = (phi_lo + phi_hi)/2; break ties by lowest beam index, so the choice is deterministic. Edge standoff delta = min(atan(r_clear / d_eval), dphi / 2 - 0.02) rad — the angle a body-clearance subtends at the aperture, floored so a just-admissible gap still yields a non-empty aim interval. Aim bearing phi_aim = clip(theta_g, phi_lo + delta, phi_hi - delta). When the goal bearing already lies well inside the gap the robot drives straight at the goal; when it lies near a jamb, the clip pushes it to the middle-safe side.
Command. wz = clip(1.5 * phi_aim, -1.0, 1.0) rad/s, with wz = 0 for |phi_aim| < 0.05 rad to avoid dithering; gain 1.5 1/s saturates the yaw limit at |phi_aim| > 0.67 rad, i.e. large heading errors are turned at full rate. vx = clip(0.8 * cos(phi_aim), 0.0, 0.8) * min(1.0, d_ahead / d_block) m/s, where d_ahead is the minimum finite range within +/-0.43 rad of phi_aim: speed falls linearly to zero as the aim direction itself closes to nothing, and the cosine stops the robot from translating fast while it is still turning far off its target. vy = 0 — strafing is not needed by this mechanism and mixing it in would confound the effect being tested. If `contact` is true, emit (vx, vy, wz) = (-0.2, 0.0, wz) for one step before resuming, so a grazing contact does not become a push.
Deliberately excluded: commitment hysteresis between competing gaps across steps. Two nearly equal gaps either side of a pillar can make this rule alternate. That is a real failure and a separate mechanism; it is a separate card, because a unit scenario cannot isolate both effects at once.

prediction:
  statement: On unmapped indoor layouts where the straight line from start to a disclosed goal is occluded by walls or furniture, replacing the goal-bearing heading command with the gap-clipped goal bearing raises the fraction of seeds on which the goal is reached, relative to the goal_seeker baseline, because the robot passes through apertures instead of stalling against the occluder face.
  metric: goal_reached
  baseline: goal_seeker
  min_effect: 0.15
  cost_metric: path_length
```

The fields mean what they say, and each one has a job:

- **mechanism** — what happens, and why it helps. This is the node body.
- **trigger** — when it applies. This is the precondition, and under the layered
  pipeline it is doing real work: outside the trigger your node must leave the
  base's command alone.
- **derivation** — how the principle becomes a rule for a Go2 with a 181-beam 2D
  scan. Where the derivation and your instincts disagree, follow the derivation:
  it is what the card is for.
- **prediction** — the falsifiable claim. **Restate it verbatim** in
  `PREDICTION`: the metric, the baseline and the minimum effect are the card's,
  not yours.
- **node_name** — what the leaf is called. Use it as the class name.

You are not told where this principle came from, and you do not need to know.
A card is a card: extracted from a paper, recalled from one, or devised from
nothing, it is implemented the same way and judged by the same harness.

If you believe a different mechanism would score better, that belief is not what
is being measured here — a node that quietly implements something else makes the
card untestable.

**If the principle genuinely cannot be expressed as an adjustment to an existing
navigator, say so in prose and write the closest honest version you can.** Some
mechanisms are whole navigators and this pipeline cannot represent them; that is
a finding about the corpus, and it is more useful than a node that pretends.

## How this node will be judged

Two steps, both automatic, neither of which you can talk round.

1. **Validity.** Your module is loaded, wired into
   `Layer[ports, BASE, your node]`, and ticked over a rollout. It has to build,
   its ports have to be satisfiable, and it must not raise. Writing a Twist
   field you did not declare fails here.
2. **Contribution.** The tree above is run over a suite of randomly generated
   indoor worlds and compared, on identical worlds, against the base alone. What
   is reported is how many worlds your node **fixed** (the base failed, the pair
   succeeded) and how many it **broke** (the reverse).

You do not write the worlds and you have never seen them. There is no
micro-world to build and no baseline to name — that is deliberate, because a
generator that writes both the mechanism and the world that judges it is
grading its own homework.

## Rules the candidate is checked against

Your module is rejected, automatically, if any of these is false. The rejection
is recorded with its reason; it is not a catastrophe, but it is a wasted node.

- It parses, and it imports **only** from this list:
  `math`, `numpy`, `core.observation`, `nodes.contract`, `harness.micro`.
  Nothing else — no `os`, no file access, no `core.scenario`, no `core.geometry`.
  Your node learns about the world through `obs`, and that restriction is what
  makes "no coupling to a specific scenario" true rather than promised.
- It defines **exactly one** `Condition`, `Action` or `Decorator` subclass.
- Every port type is one of the seven. `EFFECT` and `PRECONDITION` are non-empty.
- `WRITES` names only `vx`, `vy` and `wz`, and the node writes nothing outside
  it.

## What to return

One fenced ```python block. It contains exactly two things:

1. **One node class** — normally an `Action` with a narrowed `WRITES`.
2. **`PREDICTION`** — a module-level dict, the card's falsifiable claim:

   ```python
   PREDICTION = {
       "metric": "goal_reached",     # what gets better
       "baseline": "base",           # what it gets better than
       "min_effect": 0.5,            # by at least how much
       "cost_metric": "time_to_goal" # what it makes WORSE. Required, and honest.
   }
   ```

   `cost_metric` may be `""` only if you genuinely believe the mechanism costs
   nothing, and you should be suspicious of that belief.

**No `micro()`.** Do not write one; it is not read.

Put a short docstring on the class saying what mechanism it implements, which
Twist field it revises and why, and when it declines. Write it as you would
write code someone else has to maintain: comments where a choice is not obvious,
and no comments restating the line below them.

response.text:
This card is expressible as a modifier, with one honest compromise I want to flag up front.

**Why `adjust` and not `cap` for `vx`.** The pipeline prefers `cap` for anything shaped like a limit, and the speed term here (`0.8·cos(φ_aim) · min(1, d_ahead/d_block)`) genuinely is one. But the failure mode the card targets is the base *stalling* against an occluder face — base `vx` near zero while it grinds. A `cap` cannot lift that, so the robot would rotate toward the aperture and never translate through it, which is precisely the effect being tested. So `vx` is `adjust`ed to the derived value while the trigger holds, and `wz` is `adjust`ed because a replacement heading is what the mechanism *is*. That makes this a wide modifier — two of three fields — and it is the reason the trigger has to be narrow: goal disclosed, goal corridor actually blocked within 1.2 m, and an admissible gap present. Outside that conjunction the node writes nothing and the base passes through byte-identical.

**`vy` is deliberately not declared.** The card says `vy = 0`, but declaring a third field to zero it would make this a full navigator by the rules above, and the derivation's own reason for `vy = 0` is that strafing would confound the effect — it is a statement about what this node *doesn't* do, not a write it needs. The base keeps `vy`.

**Excluded, per the card:** cross-step commitment hysteresis between two near-equal gaps. The node will alternate around a symmetric pillar. That is a real failure, it belongs to a separate card, and papering over it here would make both effects unattributable.

```python
import math

import numpy as np

from nodes.contract import Action, Direction, Port, PortType, Status


class SteerThroughWidestAdmissibleGap(Action):
    """Gap-clipped goal bearing.

    When the straight line to a disclosed goal is occluded, this node replaces
    the commanded heading (``wz``) and the forward speed (``vx``) with a heading
    aimed at the admissible free-space opening angularly closest to the goal,
    held one body-clearance off either jamb.

    It revises ``wz`` because the mechanism *is* a heading substitution: neither
    goal-pursuit nor pure repulsion gets through an aperture narrower than the
    obstacle beside it. It revises ``vx`` because the failure being repaired is
    a stall against the occluder face -- a cap cannot restore forward motion,
    only a set can -- and because the speed must fall off as the aim direction
    itself closes.

    It declines (FAILURE, nothing written, base command byte-identical) when the
    goal has not been disclosed, when the goal corridor is not actually
    obstructed, or when no admissible gap exists in the forward half-plane.
    Those three cases belong to an explorer, a straight-line pursuit node and a
    recovery node respectively. It never returns SUCCESS; the tree's
    goal-reached condition terminates it.
    """

    WRITES = ("vx", "wz")
    PORTS = (Port("gap_aim_bearing", PortType.BEARING, Direction.OUT),)
    PRECONDITION = (
        "The goal position is disclosed and the corridor along the goal bearing "
        "is obstructed within the distance the robot needs to turn."
    )
    EFFECT = (
        "Steers along the free-space-clipped goal bearing -- the admissible gap "
        "closest to the goal, aimed one body-clearance inside its edges."
    )
    TAGS = ("gap", "steering", "occlusion", "aperture", "lidar", "subsumption")

    # Body scale: Go2 circumscribed radius ~0.38 m -> 0.40 m, plus 0.15 m margin.
    R_BODY = 0.40
    R_CLEAR = 0.55

    # Tightest commandable arc is v/w = 0.8/1.0 = 0.8 m; plus the body radius.
    D_BLOCK = 1.2
    # Half-width of the goal corridor: atan(R_CLEAR / D_BLOCK).
    CORRIDOR_HALF = 0.43
    # A beam is "free" only if the aperture does not close at the turning distance.
    D_FREE = 1.5

    # Beam spacing cannot resolve width beyond ~3 m, so cap the depth used for it.
    D_EVAL_MAX = 3.0
    # Body width 0.31 m plus ~0.145 m either side; below any real doorway (0.76 m).
    W_MIN = 0.60

    YAW_GAIN = 1.5
    YAW_MAX = 1.0
    YAW_DEADBAND = 0.05
    VX_MAX = 0.8
    VX_CONTACT = -0.2

    def reset(self, scenario, rng):
        self._last_aim = None

    # -- geometry helpers ------------------------------------------------

    @staticmethod
    def _wrap(a):
        """Wrap to (-pi, pi]; works on scalars and arrays."""
        return np.arctan2(np.sin(a), np.cos(a))

    def _scan(self, obs):
        """Angle-sorted beams with inf / over-range treated as free at range_max."""
        angles = self._wrap(np.asarray(obs.range_angles, dtype=float))
        raw = np.asarray(obs.ranges, dtype=float)
        r_max = float(obs.range_max)
        # An unreturned beam is free at this range, not unknown.
        ranges = np.where(np.isfinite(raw), raw, r_max)
        ranges = np.clip(ranges, 0.0, r_max)
        order = np.argsort(angles)
        return angles[order], ranges[order], r_max

    def _min_range_near(self, angles, ranges, center, half_width, r_max):
        mask = np.abs(self._wrap(angles - center)) <= half_width
        if not np.any(mask):
            return r_max
        return float(np.min(ranges[mask]))

    def _goal_bearing(self, obs):
        """Goal bearing in the robot frame, or None if the goal is undisclosed.

        Only the bearing is consumed and it is recomputed from scratch every
        step, so pose drift perturbs the *preference* and never the geometry.
        """
        goal = obs.goal
        if goal is None:
            return None
        gx, gy = float(goal[0]), float(goal[1])
        x, y, yaw = (float(v) for v in obs.pose_estimate)
        return float(self._wrap(math.atan2(gy - y, gx - x) - yaw))

    def _admissible_gaps(self, angles, ranges):
        """Maximal runs of free beams in the forward half-plane that fit the body.

        Returns (phi_lo, phi_hi, d_eval, index) per surviving run, where index is
        the lowest beam index of the run so selection can break ties on it.
        """
        forward = np.abs(angles) <= math.pi / 2.0
        if not np.any(forward):
            return []
        idx = np.flatnonzero(forward)
        free = ranges[idx] >= self.D_FREE

        gaps = []
        start = None
        for k in range(len(idx) + 1):
            is_free = bool(free[k]) if k < len(idx) else False
            if is_free and start is None:
                start = k
            elif not is_free and start is not None:
                gaps.append((start, k - 1))
                start = None

        out = []
        for lo_k, hi_k in gaps:
            lo_i, hi_i = idx[lo_k], idx[hi_k]
            phi_lo, phi_hi = float(angles[lo_i]), float(angles[hi_i])
            dphi = phi_hi - phi_lo
            if dphi <= 0.0:
                continue
            # Conservative depth: the shallower jamb, and never credited past 3 m.
            d_eval = min(float(ranges[lo_i]), float(ranges[hi_i]), self.D_EVAL_MAX)
            width = 2.0 * d_eval * math.sin(dphi / 2.0)
            if width >= self.W_MIN:
                out.append((phi_lo, phi_hi, d_eval, int(lo_i)))
        return out

    def _aim(self, gap, theta_g):
        """Bearing inside the gap closest to the goal, standing off both jambs."""
        phi_lo, phi_hi, d_eval, _ = gap
        dphi = phi_hi - phi_lo
        # Angle a body-clearance subtends at the aperture, floored so that a
        # just-admissible gap still leaves a non-empty aim interval.
        delta = min(math.atan2(self.R_CLEAR, max(d_eval, 1e-3)), dphi / 2.0 - 0.02)
        delta = max(delta, 0.0)
        low, high = phi_lo + delta, phi_hi - delta
        if low > high:
            return (phi_lo + phi_hi) / 2.0
        return float(min(max(theta_g, low), high))

    # -- contract --------------------------------------------------------

    def precondition(self, obs, ports):
        theta_g = self._goal_bearing(obs)
        if theta_g is None:
            return False
        angles, ranges, r_max = self._scan(obs)
        blocked = self._min_range_near(
            angles, ranges, theta_g, self.CORRIDOR_HALF, r_max
        )
        return blocked < self.D_BLOCK

    def tick(self, obs, ports):
        # Re-checked here so the node is correct even if ticked without its
        # precondition, and because (c) needs the gap set anyway.
        theta_g = self._goal_bearing(obs)
        if theta_g is None:
            return Status.FAILURE

        angles, ranges, r_max = self._scan(obs)
        if self._min_range_near(
            angles, ranges, theta_g, self.CORRIDOR_HALF, r_max
        ) >= self.D_BLOCK:
            return Status.FAILURE

        gaps = self._admissible_gaps(angles, ranges)
        if not gaps:
            return Status.FAILURE

        best = min(
            gaps,
            key=lambda g: (abs(float(self._wrap((g[0] + g[1]) / 2.0 - theta_g))), g[3]),
        )
        phi_aim = self._aim(best, theta_g)

        wz = 0.0 if abs(phi_aim) < self.YAW_DEADBAND else float(
            np.clip(self.YAW_GAIN * phi_aim, -self.YAW_MAX, self.YAW_MAX)
        )

        ports["gap_aim_bearing"] = phi_aim
        self._last_aim = phi_aim

        if obs.contact:
            # Back off a grazing touch rather than leaning into it, while still
            # turning toward the aperture.
            ports.adjust(vx=self.VX_CONTACT)
            ports.adjust(wz=wz)
            return Status.RUNNING

        d_ahead = self._min_range_near(
            angles, ranges, phi_aim, self.CORRIDOR_HALF, r_max
        )
        # cos() holds speed down while the heading error is still large; the
        # range term takes it to zero as the aim direction itself closes.
        vx = float(np.clip(self.VX_MAX * math.cos(phi_aim), 0.0, self.VX_MAX))
        vx *= min(1.0, d_ahead / self.D_BLOCK)

        ports.adjust(vx=vx)
        ports.adjust(wz=wz)
        return Status.RUNNING
```

Notes on two judgement calls inside the derivation:

- **Free-beam runs are found in the angle-sorted forward band**, so a run is contiguous in bearing rather than in raw beam order — `obs.ranges[0]` is not the front, and the 181 beams span a full circle, so sorting is what makes "maximal contiguous angular interval" mean what the card says.
- **`inf` is collapsed to `range_max` before any test**, per the derivation: an unreturned beam is free at 6 m, not unknown. This matters at the trigger too — if every beam in the goal corridor is unreturned, the corridor reads 6.0 m, the trigger fails, and straight-line pursuit correctly keeps control.

The cost is real and is the card's own: `path_length`. Routing through an aperture that is angularly off the goal bearing, and standing off both jambs rather than cutting the corner, is strictly longer than the straight line whenever the straight line happens to be passable — which is why the trigger requires the corridor to be measurably blocked first.
